title: Rank of a matrix by Echelon form

sections.heading: 2.7 (1) Rank of a Matrix
paragraphs: If we select any r rows and r columns from any matrix A, deleting all the other rows and columns, then the determinant formed by these r × r elements is called the minor of A of order r. Clearly, there will be a number of different minors of the same order, got by deleting different rows and columns from the same matrix.
Def. A matrix is said to be of rank r when
bullets: (i) it has at least one non-zero minor of order r, and
(ii) every minor of order higher than r vanishes.
Briefly, the rank of a matrix is the largest order of any non-vanishing minor of the matrix.
The rank of a matrix A shall be denoted by \(\rho(A)\).

sections.heading: Observations
bullets: Obs. 1. Rank of A and its transpose is the same i.e. \(\rho(A)=\rho(A\prime)\).
Obs. 2. Rank of a null matrix is zero.
Obs. 3. Rank of a non-singular square matrix of order r is r.
Obs. 4. If a matrix has a non-zero minor of order r, its rank is \(\ge r\). If all minors of a matrix of order \(r+1\) are zero, its rank is \(\le r\).

sections.heading: 2.7 (2) Elementary transformation of a matrix
paragraphs: The following operations, three of which refer to rows and three to columns are known as elementary transformations:
bullets: I. The interchange of any two rows (columns).
II. The multiplication of any row (column) by a non-zero number.
III. The addition of a constant multiple of the elements of any row (column) to the corresponding elements of any other row (column).

Notation. The elementary row transformations will be denoted by the following symbols: (i) \(R_{ij}\) for the interchange of the ith and jth rows. (ii) \(kR_i\) for multiplication of the ith row by k. (iii) \(R_i+pR_j\) for addition to the ith row, p times the jth row.
The corresponding column transformation will be denoted by writing C in place of R.

Elementary transformations do not change either the order or rank of a matrix. While the value of the minors may get changed by the transformation I and II, their zero or non-zero character remains unaffected.

sections.heading: 2.7 (3) Equivalent matrix
paragraphs: Two matrices A and B are said to be equivalent if one can be obtained from the other by a sequence of elementary transformations. Two equivalent matrices have the same order and the same rank. The symbol ~ is used for equivalence.

sections.heading: Normal form — class-note view
paragraphs: Normal form is also called canonical form.

A matrix in normal form contains an identity block. Matrices of the forms \([I_r\ 0]\), \(\begin{bmatrix}I_r\\0\end{bmatrix}\) and \(\begin{bmatrix}I_r&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\) are in normal form, where \(I_r\) is an identity matrix.
To reduce a matrix to normal form, both row and column transformations may be used. After reduction, \(\rho(A)\) is given by the order of the identity matrix in the normal form.

sections.heading: (2) Rouche’s theorem
paragraphs: The system of Eqn. (i) is consistent if and only if the coefficient matrix A and the augmented matrix K are of the same rank otherwise the system is inconsistent.
Proof. We consider the following two possible cases:
I. Rank of A = rank of K = r (r ≤ the smaller of the numbers m and n). The Eqn. (i) can, be suitable row operations, be reduced to
and the remaining m − r equations being all of the form 0x₁ + 0x₂ + …… + 0xₙ = 0.
The Eqn. (ii) will have a solution, though n − r of the unknowns may be chosen arbitrarily. The solution, will be unique only when r = n. Hence the Eqn. (i) are consistent.
II. Rank of A (i.e., r) < rank of K. In particular, let the rank of K be r + 1. In this case, the Eqn. (i) will reduce, by suitable row operations, to
and the remaining m − (r + 1) equations are of the form 0x₁ + 0x₂ + … + 0xₙ = 0.
Clearly, the (r + 1)th equation cannot be satisfied by any set of values for the unknowns. Hence the Eqn. (i) are inconsistent.

sections.heading: Procedure to test the consistency of a system of equations in n unknowns

book_refs.note: Procedure to test the consistency of a system of equations in n unknowns

paragraphs: Find the ranks of the coefficient matrix A and the augmented matrix K, by reducing A to the triangular form by elementary row operations. Let the rank of A be r and that of K be r′.
bullets: If r ≠ r′, the equations are inconsistent, i.e., there is no solution.
If r = r′ = n, the equations are consistent and there is a unique solution.
If r = r′ < n, the equations are consistent and there are infinite number of solutions. Giving arbitrary values to n − r of the unknowns, we may express the other r unknowns in terms of these.

sections.heading: Consistency — class-note view
paragraphs: A system is said to be consistent if it has at least one solution.
For \(AX=B\), the system is consistent if and only if \(\rho(A)=\rho(A|B)\), where \((A|B)\) is the augmented matrix.
bullets: If \(\rho(A)=\rho(A|B)=n\) (number of unknowns), the system has a unique solution.
If \(\rho(A)=\rho(A|B)<n\), the system has infinitely many solutions; \(n-r\) variables may be taken as independent parameters when the common rank is \(r\).
If \(\rho(A)\ne\rho(A|B)\), the system has no solution and is inconsistent.
A system \(AX=B\) is non-homogeneous when \(B\ne0\). A non-homogeneous system may or may not be consistent.

intro: **PankusDesk context.** Gauss–Seidel is an iterative method for solving simultaneous linear equations. Instead of obtaining the solution through one finite elimination process, we begin with approximate values and repeatedly improve them. The unknowns are calculated one after another, and each newly calculated value is used immediately in the next calculation. This is the key idea behind the textbook’s statement that Gauss–Seidel is a modification of Jacobi’s method.

paragraphs: The linear transformation \(Y=AX\) is said to be orthogonal if it transforms \(y_1^2+y_2^2+\cdots+y_n^2\) into \(x_1^2+x_2^2+\cdots+x_n^2\). The matrix of an orthogonal transformation is called an orthogonal matrix.
For the transformation to preserve the sum of squares, \(A^{T}A=I\). Therefore \(A^{T}=A^{-1}\), and hence a square matrix \(A\) is orthogonal if \(AA^{T}=A^{T}A=I\).

sections.heading: 2.14 Properties of Eigen Values
bullets: I. A square matrix \(A\) and its transpose \(A^{T}\) have the same eigenvalues, since \(|A^{T}-\lambda I|=|(A-\lambda I)^{T}|=|A-\lambda I|\).
II. The eigenvalues of a triangular matrix are its diagonal elements. Hence the eigenvalues of a diagonal matrix are just its diagonal elements.
III. The eigenvalues of an idempotent matrix are either 0 or 1. If \(A^2=A\) and \(AX=\lambda X\), then \(\lambda^2X=\lambda X\), so \(\lambda(\lambda-1)=0\).
IV. The sum of the eigenvalues of a matrix is its trace, i.e. the sum of the principal diagonal elements.
V. The product of the eigenvalues of a matrix \(A\) is equal to \(|A|\).
VI. If \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of a non-singular matrix \(A\), then \(1/\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of \(A^{-1}\).
VII. If \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of an orthogonal matrix \(A\), then \(1/\lambda\) is also an eigenvalue of \(A\), because \(A^{-1}=A^{T}\) and \(A\) and \(A^{T}\) have the same eigenvalues.

VIII. If \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots,\lambda_n\) are the eigenvalues of \(A\), then \(A^m\) has eigenvalues \(\lambda_1^m,\lambda_2^m,\ldots,\lambda_n^m\) for a positive integer \(m\); the corresponding eigenvectors remain the same.

title: Nature of the Quadratic Forms
intro: After reduction to canonical form, Grewal classifies the quadratic form by its positive and negative square terms, equivalently by the signs of the eigenvalues of its symmetric matrix.
learn: Index = number of positive terms in the canonical form.
Signature = number of positive terms minus number of negative terms.
The signs of the eigenvalues determine whether the form is positive definite, negative definite, semidefinite or indefinite.

sections.heading: 2.18 Nature of a Quadratic Form

book_refs.note: Index, signature and classification of quadratic forms

paragraphs: Let \(Q=X^{T}AX\) be a quadratic form in \(n\) variables. The number of positive terms in its canonical form is called the index. The signature is the difference between the number of positive and negative terms in the canonical form.
bullets: If the rank of \(A\) is \(r\) and the index is \(s\), the form is positive definite if \(r=n\) and \(s=n\).
It is negative definite if \(r=n\) and \(s=0\).
It is positive semidefinite if \(r<n\) and \(s=r\).
It is negative semidefinite if \(r<n\) and \(s=0\).
It is indefinite in all other cases.

Equivalently: positive definite if all eigenvalues of \(A\) are positive; negative definite if all are negative; positive semidefinite if all are non-negative with at least one zero; negative semidefinite if all are non-positive with at least one zero; indefinite if some eigenvalues are positive and others negative.
